items.title: [ScienceDaily] The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
items.content_html: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive.

items.title: [space.com] ISS astronauts install seventh upgraded solar array during 100th US spacewalk
items.content_html: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed and unfurled the International Space Station’s seventh upgraded roll-out solar array on Oct. 29, completing a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk that marked the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the station. The new panel adds about 8 kilowatts of power to support station operations as the original arrays lose output after exceeding their 15-year design life. The crew used the Canadarm2 robotic arm to move the array to its mounting point and connected it to power channel 2A. The new arrays supplement, rather than replace, the station’s original solar wings; together, they are expected to raise available power to about 215 kilowatts. The extra capacity will support research, life-support systems and visiting spacecraft through the station’s planned 2030 retirement and controlled deorbit. The crew also completed preparatory work for the eighth and final array. Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to install it on Nov. 5, completing the five-year upgrade.

items.title: [nasa.gov] 4.1-billion-year-old Mars meteorite reveals evidence of ancient water
items.content_html: NASA-funded researchers say Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali’s Sahara in 2022, formed in Mars’ crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, potentially making it the oldest of about 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth. The study, published in Science on Oct. 29, describes a rare sample from the planet’s early crust; only three known Martian meteorites date to that period. The rock is a coarse-grained igneous material called gabbro, formed as magma cooled underground. Its oxygen and hydrogen isotope signatures, along with altered minerals, indicate that water reached deep into the crust and interacted with rock more than 4.1 billion years ago; the rock itself likely formed earlier. Spacecraft observations have also shown evidence of ancient water on Mars. Researchers say the evidence supports the possibility that early Mars had habitable conditions, but does not show that life existed there. Orbital mineral data point to 13 possible source locations in the planet’s southern highlands, but the meteorite’s precise birthplace remains unknown.

items.title: [esa.int] Hubble and Webb expose hidden structures in Carina star-forming cloud
items.content_html: NASA’s Hubble and James Webb space telescopes have captured complementary views of the Cat’s Head Nebula, a star-forming pillar in the Carina Nebula about 7,500 light-years from Earth. Hubble’s visible-light image shows a dark dust column edged by glowing gas, while Webb’s infrared observations reveal details within the dust, including stars and fine strands. The images, released Oct. 29, help astronomers examine how young stars form in gas and dust exposed to radiation from massive nearby stars. Ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds likely shaped the pillar’s outline by eroding its surroundings, while denser material resisted erosion. Webb also imaged the lower-metallicity N159 star-forming region in the Large Magellanic Cloud, while Chandra and Webb observations show young stars forming in a separate Carina cloud.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
items.content_html: Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
items.content_html: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
items.content_html: NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars.

items.title: [sci.news] Cambridge study finds comets rarely delivered life’s ingredients to Earth
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

A University of Cambridge-led study finds it was extremely unlikely that comets delivered enough hydrogen cyanide, a chemical used in proposed pathways to life, to early Earth. The study, published in Scientific Reports on Oct. 28, used computer simulations to model comet evolution, atmospheric entry and impacts. The team says most impacts would destroy the molecule or fail to leave it at a useful concentration. Of the researchers’ 100,000 simulated histories, 54% included no comet impact that delivered hydrogen cyanide at concentrations considered sufficient for prebiotic chemistry. Comet delivery was more likely on Mars, where lower gravity and a thinner atmosphere make successful impacts more feasible, but the study does not establish that it happened there. The authors point to asteroid impacts or chemical processes on Earth as alternatives; outside researchers say the findings test a specific delivery pathway, not every possible comet contribution.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Antarctica’s “Doomsday Glacier” could raise sea levels twice as much as predicted
items.content_html: Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier may be melting twice as much as previously predicted, even without additional global warming. Scientists discovered that warm ocean water is penetrating miles beneath the ice, weakening its foundations and accelerating its retreat. A new model predicts that the glacier could add up to 30 millimeters to global sea levels by 2100, with a 60% chance of losing a crucial stabilizing ridge.

What we think of as the mammoth-romping, Neanderthal-stomping chapter of geological history was technically a glacial maximum, one our planet would now be returning to if not for our love of burning coal, according to a recently published study.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought
items.content_html: A major new study reveals that autistic children’s brains process faces differently, and those differences may begin earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that brain signals associated with recognizing faces become more specialized as neurotypical children grow older, but show much less change in autistic children. The discovery could help explain why some autistic people have difficulty recognizing faces and reading emotions.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
items.content_html: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
items.content_html: Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Triassic armored amphibian fossils point to life entirely at sea
items.content_html: Researchers have described Gerrothorax maritimus, an armored amphibian that may have lived its entire life in the sea about 237 million years ago. The claim rests on two nearly complete skeletons found in marine deposits in Guizhou, China, more than 30 kilometers from nearby islands. Their preserved limbs and strontium isotope signatures are consistent with the animals having lived and grown in seawater. The study appeared in Nature Ecology & Evolution on Oct. 26. The roughly 74-centimeter-long animal had a flattened body covered in bony armor. Researchers propose that the armor limited water exchange through its skin, while its gills and digestive tract may have helped it cope with salt. Its skull shape suggests it waited on the seafloor and sucked in prey. No living amphibian is known to live exclusively in the ocean, and fewer than 2% of modern amphibian species show any salt tolerance.

items.content_html: Regular exercise does more than strengthen the heart. New research reveals that it actually reshapes the nerves controlling how the heart functions, and the changes are surprisingly different on the left and right sides of the body.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
items.content_html: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.
